questions.q: The genetic material of bacteriophage T4 is:
questions.x: T4 has a linear double-stranded DNA molecule packed in its polyhedral head, which it injects into the bacterium.

questions.q: The common cold is most often caused by:
questions.x: Rhinoviruses infect the lining of the nose and are the commonest cause of the common cold. Rotaviruses cause diarrhoea in children.

questions.q: The chemiosmotic theory of ATP synthesis was proposed by:
questions.x: Peter Mitchell proposed that a proton gradient across a membrane drives ATP synthesis. Krebs described the citric acid cycle, Calvin the dark reactions of photosynthesis, and Fischer the lock-and-key model.

questions.q: Hydrolysis of one triglyceride molecule produces:
o: Three glycerol and one fatty acid
One glycerol and one fatty acid
One glycerol and three fatty acids
Two glycerol and three fatty acids
questions.x: A triglyceride is one glycerol esterified with three fatty acids, so complete hydrolysis releases one glycerol and three fatty acid molecules.

questions.q: On complete hydrolysis, a simple protein such as albumin yields:
questions.x: A simple protein is made only of amino acids. Conjugated proteins also give a non-protein part: sugars from glycoproteins, lipids from lipoproteins, nucleotides from nucleoproteins.

questions.q: Which of the following hormones is a steroid, made from cholesterol?
questions.x: Testosterone is a steroid hormone and so is a lipid. Insulin, glucagon and growth hormone are protein (peptide) hormones.

questions.q: During protein synthesis, mRNA, tRNA and rRNA all work together at the:
questions.x: Translation takes place on ribosomes, made of rRNA and protein, where mRNA codons pair with tRNA anticodons. The nucleolus only makes rRNA.

questions.q: In the human body, fat is stored mainly in:
questions.x: Adipose tissue is made of fat cells that store triglycerides under the skin and around organs. Red bone marrow makes blood cells, and cartilage is a supporting tissue.

questions.q: Compared with glycogen, triglyceride is a better long-term energy store partly because, being insoluble in water, it:
o: Is broken down faster when energy is needed suddenly
Can be carried freely in blood plasma
Has no osmotic effect and is stored without extra water
questions.x: Insoluble triglyceride does not affect the water potential of cells and is stored compactly without bound water. It is mobilised more slowly than glycogen and needs lipoproteins for transport in blood.

questions.q: Two triglyceride molecules are completely hydrolysed. How many water molecules are used, and how many fatty acid molecules are released?
questions.x: Each triglyceride has three ester bonds, so it needs three water molecules and releases three fatty acids (plus one glycerol). Two molecules therefore use 6 water and give 6 fatty acids.

questions.q: Apart from Franklin's X-ray photographs, another key piece of evidence used by Watson and Crick was:
questions.x: Chargaff had shown A = T and G = C in DNA. Watson and Crick explained these ratios by specific base pairing in their model.

questions.q: During digestion, starch is broken into glucose, proteins into amino acids and fats into fatty acids and glycerol. The main importance of this is that:
o: The body's own proteins are then made directly from the food proteins without change
Glucose can then be stored in the gut as cellulose
Food molecules become larger and so release more energy
Small soluble molecules can be absorbed and then used to build the body's own macromolecules
questions.x: Large food molecules cannot cross the gut lining, so they are hydrolysed into small units. These are absorbed and reassembled into the body's own proteins, glycogen and fats or respired.

questions.q: Which class of biological molecules is NOT a true polymer built from a long chain of repeating monomers?
questions.x: Fats and oils are made of glycerol joined to a few fatty acids, not a long chain of repeating units. Proteins, polysaccharides and nucleic acids are true polymers of amino acids, monosaccharides and nucleotides.

questions.q: HIV has RNA as its genetic material and copies it into DNA inside the host cell using the enzyme:
questions.x: Retroviruses such as HIV carry reverse transcriptase, which makes DNA from an RNA template. RNA polymerase does the reverse, making RNA from DNA.

questions.q: Ribose is an aldopentose, while ribulose is a:
questions.x: Both have five carbons, but ribulose has a ketone group, so it is a ketopentose. Ribose has an aldehyde group.

questions.q: Which amino acid is coded by only one codon?
questions.x: Tryptophan has the single codon UGG. Leucine and serine each have six codons and glycine has four, which shows the degeneracy of the code.

questions.q: Some bacteria, such as Bacillus and Clostridium, survive boiling and drying by forming:
questions.x: Endospores are tough, dormant structures formed inside the cell, which resist heat, drying and chemicals. A capsule protects against phagocytosis but not against boiling.

questions.q: Cilia and flagella of eukaryotic cells show a pattern of microtubules in cross-section described as:
questions.x: The shaft of a cilium or flagellum has nine outer doublets around two central microtubules (9 + 2). The 9 triplet pattern is seen in centrioles and basal bodies.

questions.q: Besides DNA and histones, chromosomes also contain small amounts of:
questions.x: Chromosomes are mostly DNA and histones, with small amounts of RNA and non-histone proteins such as enzymes and regulatory proteins.

questions.q: Chromosomes other than the sex chromosomes are called:
questions.x: Autosomes are all chromosomes except the sex chromosomes (X and Y); humans have 44 autosomes. Sex chromosomes are also called allosomes.

questions.q: A withdrawal reflex arc with interneurons, compared with the knee-jerk arc, must have:
o: Fewer synapses and so a faster response
No synapses inside the spinal cord
More synapses and so a longer delay
Its centre in the brain instead of the spinal cord
questions.x: Each interneuron adds a synapse, and each synapse adds a short delay, so the polysynaptic withdrawal arc is slower than the monosynaptic knee jerk. Both are spinal reflexes.

questions.q: In a reflex arc, the part of the central nervous system that receives the sensory impulse and sends out the motor impulse acts as the:
questions.x: The brain or spinal cord acts as the integrating (coordinating) centre, linking the incoming sensory impulse to an outgoing motor impulse. The receptor detects the stimulus and the effector responds.

questions.q: At the junction between the motor neuron of a spinal reflex and the skeletal muscle it supplies, the neurotransmitter released is:
questions.x: Motor neurons release acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction, which makes the skeletal muscle fibre contract. Noradrenaline is released by sympathetic nerve endings, not at skeletal muscle.

questions.q: After severe damage to the cerebral cortex, a patient is unconscious, yet breathes normally and has a regular heartbeat. This is because:
o: The cerebellum has taken over the control of breathing
The cerebral cortex is the only centre for breathing and heartbeat
The breathing and heart centres in the medulla oblongata are still working
The thalamus controls breathing and heartbeat
questions.x: Breathing and heart rate are controlled by centres in the medulla oblongata, not by the cortex. As long as the medulla is intact these vital functions continue, even when consciousness is lost.

questions.q: Thick axons conduct impulses faster than thin ones mainly because:
o: The wider axoplasm offers less resistance to the local currents
Their membranes have no ion channels
questions.x: A larger diameter lowers the internal resistance, so local currents spread further and faster, bringing the next region to threshold sooner.

questions.q: A man once stung by a bee now flinches whenever he hears buzzing nearby. He also blinks when a bee touches his eyelid. The flinch and the blink are, respectively:
questions.x: Flinching at the buzzing sound is learned from the earlier sting, so it is conditioned. Blinking when the eyelid is touched is inborn, so it is unconditioned.

questions.q: During repolarisation of the axon membrane, the voltage-gated Na+ channels:
o: Allow K+ to enter the axon
questions.x: At the peak the Na+ channels close and K+ channels open; K+ leaving the axon brings the potential back to negative.

questions.q: The ventral root of a spinal nerve contains mainly the axons of:
questions.x: Motor axons leave the spinal cord through the ventral root. Sensory fibres enter through the dorsal root, whose ganglion holds their cell bodies.

questions.q: A competitive inhibitor attaches to the enzyme:
o: Reversibly, at an allosteric site only
questions.x: Competitive inhibitors occupy the active site by weak bonds and can leave again, which is why excess substrate can displace them.

questions.q: Which of these enzymes has the highest optimum pH?
questions.x: Arginase works best at about pH 9.7, which is strongly alkaline. Pepsin's optimum is about 2, salivary amylase about 6.8 and catalase about 7.6.

questions.q: In many reactions, a coenzyme helps the enzyme by:
o: Forming the protein of the active site
Supplying amino acids for the enzyme
Carrying atoms or groups, such as hydrogen, from one reaction to another
questions.x: Coenzymes act as carriers; for example, NAD⁺ picks up hydrogen in one reaction and passes it on in another.

questions.q: A mutation alters only the catalytic site of an enzyme; its binding site is normal. The most likely result is that:
o: The substrate can no longer bind
The substrate still binds but is not converted into products
The enzyme works faster than before
questions.x: The binding site attaches the substrate, but the catalytic site does the chemical change. With a faulty catalytic site the substrate is held but not changed.

questions.q: Chloride ions increase the activity of salivary amylase. Here chloride is acting as:
questions.x: Small inorganic ions that increase an enzyme's activity are called activators; chloride ions activate salivary amylase. An inhibitor would reduce activity.

questions.q: In a herd of gazelles, the fastest runners escape cheetahs more often. Over many generations, what is expected?
o: Every gazelle becomes faster by training
The herd stops varying in speed
The average running speed of the herd increases
questions.x: Faster gazelles survive and breed more, so alleles for speed become more common and the average speed rises. Training effects are not inherited.

questions.q: A common misunderstanding of Darwin's theory is the claim that natural selection:
o: Acts on variations that already exist
Works only on variations that are inherited
Leads to populations better suited to their environment
Produces the variations that an organism needs
questions.x: Natural selection does not create variation; variation arises from mutation and recombination. Selection only favours some existing variants over others.

questions.q: According to the endosymbiotic theory, mitochondria were originally:
o: Aerobic bacteria taken into a larger host cell
questions.x: The endosymbiotic theory says mitochondria came from aerobic bacteria, and chloroplasts from cyanobacteria, that lived inside a larger cell and became permanent partners. This helps explain the origin of eukaryotic cells.

questions.q: The thick muscular layer of the uterine wall that contracts strongly during childbirth is the:
questions.x: The myometrium is the smooth muscle layer of the uterus. The endometrium is the inner lining that thickens each cycle and receives the embryo.

questions.q: Antibiotics such as penicillin cure syphilis but have no effect on genital herpes or HIV. The reason is that:
o: Viruses lack the bacterial structures, such as cell walls and 70S ribosomes, that antibiotics attack
Herpes and HIV live only outside cells
Antibiotics are destroyed by the immune system
questions.x: Antibiotics target features of bacteria, such as cell-wall synthesis or 70S ribosomes. Viruses have none of these and multiply inside host cells.

questions.q: Which statement about the two types of herpes simplex virus is correct?
o: HSV-1 causes syphilis, while HSV-2 causes gonorrhoea
HSV-2 mainly causes genital herpes, while HSV-1 mainly causes cold sores around the mouth
Both types cause only skin rashes on the palms
questions.x: HSV-2 is the usual cause of genital herpes and HSV-1 of oral cold sores, though each can infect either site.

questions.q: Which male gland contributes the largest share of the volume of semen?
questions.x: The seminal vesicles supply most of the fluid volume of semen (roughly 60%). The testes provide the sperm but only a small part of the volume.

questions.q: How does osteoarthritis typically develop over time?
o: Suddenly overnight after a heavy meal
Within days after bacteria enter the joint
Mainly in early childhood, then disappears
questions.x: Osteoarthritis develops gradually as joint cartilage wears down over years. A sudden attack after a heavy meal suggests gout, and bacterial infection causes septic arthritis.

questions.q: A supporting tissue has cells in lacunae, a matrix full of thick collagen bundles and no perichondrium. It was most probably taken from the:
questions.x: Thick collagen bundles and no perichondrium identify fibrocartilage, found in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs. The pinna and epiglottis are elastic cartilage and the nose is hyaline.

questions.q: Bone is a living tissue, not just a dead mineral frame. Evidence for this is that bone:
o: Loses all its cells once the matrix is mineralised
Has blood vessels and nerves and can repair a fracture
Keeps the same matrix unchanged throughout life
Receives nutrients only by diffusion from cartilage
questions.x: Bone is well supplied with blood vessels and nerves, its cells stay alive in lacunae, and it is constantly remodelled and can heal fractures.

questions.q: An oval, rounded bone end fits into an oval hollow. The joint bends forward and backward and side to side, but cannot rotate. This joint is a:
questions.x: An oval surface in an oval hollow gives movement in two planes without rotation: a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint. A ball-and-socket joint would also allow rotation, and a pivot allows rotation only.

questions.q: Which is a function of cartilage rather than of bone?
o: Storing most of the body's calcium
Acting as rigid levers for movement
Giving flexible support that bends and springs back
questions.x: Cartilage gives firm but flexible support, as in the pinna and nose. Blood cell production, calcium storage and acting as levers are functions of bone.

questions.q: Swinging the arm round in a full circle (circumduction) is possible at the shoulder because it is a:
questions.x: A ball-and-socket joint allows movement in all planes, so the limb can trace a circle. Hinge joints move in one plane, pivot joints only rotate, and gliding joints only slide.

questions.q: The small joints between the articular processes of neighbouring vertebrae, where flat surfaces slide on each other, are:
questions.x: These joints have flat facing surfaces that slide a little, so they are gliding (plane) synovial joints. The vertebral bodies themselves are joined by cartilaginous intervertebral discs.

questions.q: All the tall plants of a monohybrid F2 (from Tt × Tt) are self-pollinated, each giving equal numbers of offspring. What fraction of the resulting F3 plants is expected to be dwarf?
questions.x: Of the tall F2 plants, 1/3 are TT (no dwarf offspring) and 2/3 are Tt (1/4 dwarf offspring). Dwarf fraction = 2/3 × 1/4 = 1/6.

questions.q: Two human genes lie on chromosome 3 and chromosome 11 respectively. These two genes:
questions.x: Linkage applies only to genes on the same chromosome. Genes on different chromosomes belong to different linkage groups and assort independently.

questions.q: A colour-blind woman and a man with normal vision have a daughter. This daughter marries a man with normal vision. What is the probability that a son of hers is colour-blind?
questions.x: The daughter got Xᶜ from her mother and a normal X from her father, so she is certainly a carrier. Each of her sons has a 1/2 chance of receiving Xᶜ.

questions.q: A pea plant of genotype Tt forms gametes. In what proportion are they produced?
o: Half carry T and half carry t
Three quarters carry T and one quarter carry t
All carry both T and t
questions.x: By the law of segregation the two alleles separate at meiosis, so each gamete gets one allele and T and t gametes form in equal numbers. No gamete carries both.

questions.q: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes that must happen before crossing over, begins in which substage of prophase I?
questions.x: Homologues begin pairing in zygotene; crossing over follows in pachytene. In leptotene the chromosomes are only starting to condense, and in diplotene they begin to separate at the chiasmata.

questions.q: Ignoring crossing over, how many different combinations of maternal and paternal chromosomes can independent assortment produce in human gametes (n = 23)?
questions.x: Each of the 23 pairs can orient in two ways, independently of the others, so the number of combinations is 2²³, about 8.4 million. This is a major source of variation.

questions.q: Which observation shows that the white-eye gene of Drosophila is NOT on the Y chromosome?
o: The first white-eyed fly Morgan found was a male
White-eyed males can have white-eyed offspring
Male flies carry only one X chromosome
questions.x: Females have no Y chromosome, so a Y-linked trait could never appear in them. White-eyed females therefore show the gene is not on the Y but on the X. A white-eyed male, or a male passing the trait on, would fit Y-linkage too.

questions.q: Tall (T) is completely dominant over dwarf (t). Which cross gives a 3 : 1 phenotypic ratio among the offspring?
questions.x: Tt × Tt gives 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt, which is 3 tall : 1 dwarf. Tt × tt gives 1 : 1, and any cross with a TT parent gives only tall offspring.

questions.q: A blood clot blocks a branch of a coronary artery. The direct result is that:
o: Blood can no longer enter the right atrium
Part of the heart muscle is starved of oxygen and may die
questions.x: Coronary arteries supply the myocardium itself. A blockage cuts off oxygen to the muscle it supplies, which can die (a heart attack). The chambers, valves and lungs are not directly blocked.

questions.q: Which description fits the muscle of the heart wall?
questions.x: Cardiac muscle is striated like skeletal muscle, but its fibres branch and it is involuntary. Unstriated spindle-shaped cells describe smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which part of the digestive tract contains a large amount of lymphoid tissue?
questions.x: The appendix wall is rich in lymphoid tissue. The gall bladder stores bile, and the oesophagus and pancreatic duct are not lymphoid structures.

questions.q: Which of these vessels has NO valves?
questions.x: Capillaries are tiny tubes of a single cell layer with no valves. Limb veins and lymph vessels have valves that stop backflow.

questions.q: Unlike blood, lymph has no heart to pump it. As a result, lymph flows:
o: Faster than blood in the arteries
In both directions in each vessel
Only when a person is asleep
questions.x: With no pump, lymph moves slowly at low pressure, helped by muscle movements, with valves keeping it flowing one way.

questions.q: Besides virus-infected cells, cytotoxic T cells can also destroy:
o: The body's normal red blood cells
questions.x: Cytotoxic T cells recognise and kill body cells showing abnormal or foreign antigens, such as cancer cells. Healthy self cells are normally left alone.

questions.q: Vaccines are given before a person meets the disease mainly because:
o: Active immunity takes days to weeks to develop
Vaccines cure a disease that has already started
Vaccines work only in sick people
questions.x: A vaccine makes the body produce its own antibodies and memory cells, and this takes time. Given in advance, it ensures protection is ready when the real pathogen arrives.

questions.q: Sneezing clears irritants from the nasal cavity, whereas coughing clears them mainly from the:
questions.x: Coughing is a reflex set off by irritation of the larynx, trachea and bronchi; a forceful blast of air drives the irritant out through the mouth. Particles in the alveoli are removed by macrophages instead.

questions.q: Compared with inhaled air, exhaled air contains roughly:
questions.x: Inhaled air has about 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide. Exhaled air has about 16% oxygen and 4% carbon dioxide, and is also warmer and saturated with water vapour.

questions.q: About what proportion of the carbon dioxide in blood is carried simply dissolved in the plasma?
questions.x: Only a small share (about 7%) of CO₂ travels dissolved. Roughly a quarter is carried as carbaminohaemoglobin and the large majority as hydrogencarbonate (bicarbonate) ions.

questions.q: The cells lining the bronchi that are damaged by tobacco smoke are mainly:
questions.x: The bronchi are lined by ciliated columnar epithelium with goblet cells. Smoke paralyses and destroys the cilia and later these lining cells may become cancerous.

questions.q: Which statement about the oesophagus is correct?
o: Its glands secrete mucus but no digestive enzymes
It secretes amylase to continue starch digestion
It absorbs water and simple sugars
Its wall has no muscle, so food falls by gravity
questions.x: The oesophagus only carries food to the stomach. Its glands make mucus for lubrication; it secretes no enzymes, absorbs nothing, and moves food by peristalsis, not gravity.

questions.q: Gastric juice begins to flow when a hungry person merely sees or smells food. This early secretion is caused by:
o: Nerve impulses from the brain to the stomach (a reflex)
questions.x: The sight, smell, taste or thought of food sends nerve impulses from the brain to the gastric glands before any food arrives. Stretching and gastrin act later, once food is in the stomach, and secretin acts on the pancreas.

questions.q: A known risk of peritoneal dialysis is:
o: Rejection of the fluid by the immune system
Formation of kidney stones in the catheter
Infection of the lining of the abdominal cavity (peritonitis)
Loss of red blood cells into the fluid
questions.x: Fluid is put into the abdomen through a catheter, so bacteria can enter and infect the peritoneum. Cells cannot cross the membrane.

questions.q: When an amino acid is deaminated, the part left after removing the amino group can be:
o: Respired for energy or converted to glucose or fat
questions.x: Only the nitrogen-containing group becomes ammonia and then urea. The remaining carbon skeleton is used in respiration or stored as glucose or fat.

questions.q: Urine leaving the collecting ducts at the tip (papilla) of a renal pyramid passes first into a:
o: Calyx (cup-like branch) of the renal pelvis
questions.x: Collecting ducts open at the papilla of each pyramid into a calyx, a cup-like branch of the renal pelvis. From the pelvis urine flows down the ureter.

questions.q: Which feature is shared by both glomerular and peritubular capillaries?
o: A supply from the afferent arteriole
A pressure high enough to force fluid out along their whole length
Walls made of a single layer of endothelial cells
questions.x: Like all capillaries, both have walls one cell thick. Only the glomerulus is fed by the afferent arteriole, has high pressure throughout and lies inside the capsule.

questions.q: Which pairing of an animal with its chief excretory product is wrong?
questions.x: Birds such as sparrows excrete uric acid, not urea. The other three pairs are correct.

questions.q: Some hours after a very protein-rich meal, which change is expected?
o: Uric acid crystals in the joints
questions.x: Surplus amino acids from the meal are deaminated and their nitrogen is turned into urea, so urinary urea rises.

questions.q: The fluid that collects in the space of Bowman's capsule is called:
questions.x: Fluid forced out of the glomerulus into the capsule is glomerular filtrate. It becomes urine only after reabsorption and secretion along the tubule.

questions.q: Ammonia must be removed quickly because even a small build-up in the blood:
o: Upsets the pH and harms nerve cells, especially in the brain
Increases the oxygen carried by haemoglobin
questions.x: Ammonia is very soluble and alkaline. Small amounts disturb pH and interfere with nerve function, so land animals convert it quickly to less toxic urea.

questions.q: A dangerous fall of core body temperature below normal, for example after long exposure to cold, is called:
questions.x: Hypo means below. Hyperthermia and fever are rises in temperature; hibernation is a controlled state in some animals.

questions.q: After genetically modified yeast cells have made the viral surface protein for a vaccine, the next stage of production is to:
o: Inject the yeast cells directly into people
Insert the protein gene into a plasmid
Cut the yeast DNA with restriction enzymes
Break open the cells and purify the protein
questions.x: Downstream processing separates the wanted protein from the yeast cells and their other contents, giving a pure antigen for the vaccine. Inserting the gene and cutting DNA are earlier steps.

questions.q: In a later method of making recombinant insulin, bacteria produce a single chain, proinsulin. Proinsulin is converted to active insulin by:
o: Using enzymes to cut out the connecting C-peptide
Joining it to a second proinsulin chain
Adding a haem group to it
questions.x: Proinsulin is one chain in which the two insulin chains are linked by a C-peptide. Enzymes remove this connecting piece, leaving the two insulin chains joined by disulphide bridges.

questions.q: In a pregnancy test strip, the test line turns coloured when hCG is present because:
o: hCG itself is coloured and sticks to the strip
Urine reacts with the strip to make hCG
The fixed antibodies change colour on contact with any urine
hCG attached to coloured, mobile antibodies is trapped by fixed antibodies at the test line
questions.x: Mobile antibodies carrying a coloured label bind hCG and move up the strip; fixed antibodies at the test line capture the hCG–antibody complex, so colour builds up there. Without hCG the labelled antibodies pass on to the control line only.

questions.q: A harmless virus carrying a normal gene is injected straight into a patient's eye to treat an inherited form of blindness. This approach is described as:
questions.x: The gene is delivered directly into body cells inside the patient, so it is in vivo; only somatic (eye) cells are changed, so it is not inherited. Ex vivo therapy treats cells outside the body and returns them.

questions.q: A product has a theoretical yield of 10 g. During filtering and washing, 2 g of it is lost and nothing else goes wrong. The percentage yield is:
questions.x: Actual yield = 10 − 2 = 8 g, so percentage yield = 8/10 × 100 = 80%. 20% is the percentage lost, not the yield.

questions.q: Each sandwich needs 2 slices of bread and 1 slice of cheese. With 10 slices of bread and 4 slices of cheese, the 'limiting reactant' and the number of sandwiches are:
questions.x: Bread is enough for 10/2 = 5 sandwiches but cheese only for 4, so cheese runs out first and limits the 'product' to 4 sandwiches, leaving 2 slices of bread in excess.

questions.q: How many electrons of an atom could share the values n = 4 and m = 0?
questions.x: For n = 4, l = 0, 1, 2, 3 and each l has exactly one orbital with m = 0. That is 4 orbitals × 2 electrons = 8.

questions.q: Which was a limitation of Bohr's atomic model?
o: It could not explain the line spectrum of hydrogen
It could not explain the spectra of atoms having more than one electron
It could not account for the stability of the hydrogen atom
It could not calculate the radius of hydrogen's first orbit
questions.x: Bohr's model worked for hydrogen and one-electron ions, including the orbit radius and the line spectrum, but failed for multi-electron atoms.

questions.q: Which two ions found in positive rays have the same e/m ratio? (H = 1, He = 4)
questions.x: e/m of He²⁺ = 2/4 = 1/2 and of H₂⁺ = 1/2, so they are equal. H⁺ has 1/1, He⁺ has 1/4, so the other pairs differ.

questions.q: The gas constant R has the value 8.314 when it is expressed in:
questions.x: 1 joule = 1 newton metre, so 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ is the same as 8.314 N m K⁻¹ mol⁻¹. In the other units R is 0.0821, 1.987 and 82.1.

questions.q: A partly blown-up balloon is put in a freezer and it shrinks. According to the kinetic theory, this is because the gas molecules:
o: Slow down, so at the same outside pressure the gas takes up less space
Become larger and stick to the balloon wall
Escape through the rubber in the cold
questions.x: Cooling lowers the average speed of the molecules, so they push on the balloon wall less. The balloon shrinks until the inside pressure again matches the outside pressure.

questions.q: A gas is heated at constant pressure from 200 K to 300 K. Its volume increases by:
questions.x: V₂/V₁ = 300/200 = 1.5, so the volume rises by 50%. The 33% answer comes from dividing the change by the final temperature instead of the starting one.

questions.q: HCl (36.5 g mol⁻¹) has a larger molar mass than HF (20 g mol⁻¹), yet HF has the higher boiling point. The reason is that:
o: HCl molecules are linked by hydrogen bonds
HF has stronger London forces than HCl
The H–F covalent bond must break when HF boils
HF molecules are associated through hydrogen bonds
questions.x: Hydrogen bonds hold HF molecules together, so extra energy is needed to separate them. HCl has only weaker dipole–dipole and London forces.

questions.q: Which picture of particle motion in a liquid is correct?
o: Molecules move randomly and slide past one another
Molecules stay in fixed places and only vibrate
Molecules fly freely far apart with no attractions
Molecules are completely at rest unless heated
questions.x: In a liquid, molecules are close together but keep moving randomly and slide past each other. Fixed vibrating positions describe solids; free, distant molecules describe gases.

questions.q: Sulphur has a transition temperature of 95.5 °C. Which form of sulphur is the stable one at room temperature?
questions.x: Below 95.5 °C rhombic sulphur is stable; above it monoclinic sulphur is stable. Only at the transition temperature are both stable together.

questions.q: Most of the ammonia made by the Haber process is used to manufacture:
o: Fertilisers such as urea and ammonium salts
questions.x: The main use of ammonia is in nitrogen fertilisers such as urea, ammonium nitrate and ammonium sulphate.

questions.q: When the solubility of a salt is lowered by adding a common ion at constant temperature, its Ksp:
questions.x: Solubility falls, but Ksp is a constant at a given temperature; the ion concentrations simply readjust so their product still equals Ksp.

questions.q: The concentration of the undissolved solid is not included in a Ksp expression because:
o: The concentration of a pure solid is constant
The solid does not take part in the equilibrium
questions.x: The solid does take part in the equilibrium, but its concentration (its density over its molar mass) is constant, so it is absorbed into Ksp.

questions.q: In CH₃COOC₂H₅ + NaOH → CH₃COONa + C₂H₅OH, fast-moving OH⁻ ions are replaced by slower CH₃COO⁻ ions. The rate of this reaction can be followed by measuring the change in:
questions.x: As OH⁻ is replaced by the less mobile ethanoate ion, the conductivity of the solution falls. No gas, colour or optically active substance is involved.

questions.q: A glowing splint bursts into flame in pure oxygen but only glows in air. The factor responsible is:
o: The presence of a catalyst in pure oxygen
A lower temperature in pure oxygen
Light given off by pure oxygen
questions.x: Air is only about one-fifth oxygen. In pure oxygen the concentration of O₂ molecules is much higher, so collisions with the hot wood are more frequent.

questions.q: The activated complex is also called the:
questions.x: The activated complex is the transition state: the unstable arrangement of atoms at the top of the energy barrier.

questions.q: Aluminium powder reacts with iron(III) oxide (the thermite reaction) to give so much heat that the iron formed is molten. This reaction is:
o: Endothermic, but heat is released from the iron
questions.x: The thermite reaction gives out enough heat to melt iron, which is why it is used for welding rails. Heat given out means ΔH is negative.

questions.q: In the FSc convention, standard enthalpy changes are measured at a pressure of:
questions.x: In the FSc convention, standard conditions are 298 K and 1 atm pressure (101.325 kPa), with solutions at 1 mol dm⁻³.

questions.q: E°(Cu²⁺/Cu) = +0.34 V. When a copper electrode in 1 mol dm⁻³ Cu²⁺ is connected to the standard hydrogen electrode, the SHE acts as the:
o: Cathode, where H⁺ is reduced to H₂
Anode, where H₂ is oxidised to H⁺
Anode, where H⁺ is reduced to H₂
questions.x: Copper has the more positive E°, so Cu²⁺ is reduced at the copper cathode; the SHE therefore becomes the anode, where hydrogen is oxidised.

questions.q: Aqueous copper(II) sulphate is electrolysed using copper electrodes. What happens at the anode?
o: Oxygen gas is given off and the anode is unchanged
Copper is deposited and the anode gains mass
Copper atoms are oxidised to Cu²⁺ and the anode loses mass
Sulphate ions are reduced to sulphur dioxide
questions.x: With a copper anode, copper itself is oxidised (Cu → Cu²⁺ + 2e⁻) more easily than water, so the anode dissolves while copper deposits on the cathode.

questions.q: SO₂ has a dipole moment but SO₃ does not. This is because:
o: S–O bonds in SO₃ are non-polar
SO₂ is bent, while SO₃ is trigonal planar and symmetrical
SO₂ is linear, while SO₃ is pyramidal
Sulphur is more electronegative than oxygen in SO₃
questions.x: In planar SO₃ the three S–O dipoles at 120° cancel. In bent SO₂ the two S–O dipoles add up to a net dipole.

questions.q: In which of the following species are all the bond angles equal to 120°?
questions.x: The carbonate ion has three bonding regions and no lone pair on carbon, so it is trigonal planar with 120° angles. PCl₅ has both 120° and 90° angles; NH₃ and H₃O⁺ are pyramidal.

questions.q: Dry hydrogen chloride gas does not conduct electricity, but its solution in water does. This is because HCl:
o: Is an ionic compound in the gas state
Is a polar molecule that ionises in water into H₃O⁺ and Cl⁻ ions
Becomes non-polar when dissolved in water
Reacts with water to form chlorine gas
questions.x: HCl is a polar covalent molecule. Polar water molecules pull it apart into ions, and the ions carry the current.

questions.q: Potassium superoxide, KO₂, is used in breathing equipment in submarines and spacecraft because it:
o: Absorbs oxygen and releases carbon dioxide
Absorbs water vapour and releases hydrogen
Absorbs carbon dioxide and releases oxygen
questions.x: 4KO₂ + 2CO₂ → 2K₂CO₃ + 3O₂: exhaled CO₂ is removed and fresh oxygen is supplied.

questions.q: Which oxide of carbon is a neutral oxide?
questions.x: CO neither forms an acid with water nor reacts with bases under normal conditions. CO₂ and SiO₂ are acidic, and PbO is amphoteric.

questions.q: In the complex ion [Fe(CN)₆]⁴⁻, each cyanide ligand carries a charge of −1. The d-electron configuration of iron (Z = 26) in this ion is:
questions.x: Fe + 6(−1) = −4 gives Fe = +2, and Fe²⁺ is [Ar] 3d⁶. Taking iron as +3 would wrongly give 3d⁵.

questions.q: Which of the following is an alicyclic compound?
questions.x: Cyclopentane has a ring of carbon atoms only and behaves like an alkane, so it is alicyclic. Benzene is aromatic, pyridine heterocyclic and hexane open-chain.

questions.q: The name pent-4-ene is incorrect. The correct IUPAC name of this compound is:
questions.x: pent-4-ene numbers the chain from the wrong end. Numbering from the end nearer the double bond gives it the locant 1: pent-1-ene.

questions.q: Benzene, C₆H₆, has the same empirical formula as:
questions.x: Both C₆H₆ and C₂H₂ reduce to the empirical formula CH. Ethene and cyclohexane reduce to CH₂.

questions.q: Fluoromethane is not made by mixing methane directly with fluorine because:
o: Fluorine does not react with methane at all
The reaction needs a nickel catalyst
The reaction is explosive and hard to control
Fluorine adds to methane instead of substituting
questions.x: Fluorine is the most reactive halogen, and its reaction with methane is violent, even explosive. Methane has no multiple bond, so addition is not possible.

questions.q: In the arenium ion formed during electrophilic substitution, how many π electrons remain delocalised, and over how many carbon atoms?
questions.x: Two of benzene's six π electrons form the new bond to the electrophile, and that carbon becomes sp³. The remaining 4 π electrons and the positive charge are spread over the other 5 carbons.

questions.q: In the preparation of ethene from ethanol, concentrated H₂SO₄ acts as:
o: A dehydrating agent that removes water
An oxidising agent that removes hydrogen
A reducing agent that adds hydrogen
A source of sulphur for the product
questions.x: Concentrated H₂SO₄ removes a water molecule from ethanol, leaving the C=C bond of ethene. No oxidation or reduction of the carbon chain occurs.

questions.q: In the molecular orbital treatment of benzene, the six p orbitals combine to form six π molecular orbitals. In the ground state, the six π electrons occupy:
o: All six molecular orbitals, one electron each
questions.x: Six p orbitals give three bonding and three antibonding π orbitals. The six π electrons fill the three bonding orbitals in pairs, which makes benzene very stable.

questions.q: To saturate 14 g of ethene fully with H₂ over nickel, the mass of hydrogen required is: (C 12, H 1)
questions.x: 14 g of C₂H₄ is 14/28 = 0.5 mol, which needs 0.5 mol H₂. 0.5 × 2 = 1 g.

questions.q: By IUPAC rules, CH₃CHBrCHBrCH₃ is named:
questions.x: The chain has four carbons with bromine on the second and third carbons, giving 2,3-dibromobutane. Propane would have only three carbons.

questions.q: Bromoethane is warmed with aqueous potassium hydroxide. The main organic product is:
questions.x: In water, OH⁻ acts as a nucleophile and replaces the bromine, giving CH₃CH₂OH. Ethene is the main product with alcoholic KOH instead.

questions.q: An ester, CH₃COOCH₂CH₂CH₃, was made by heating a carboxylic acid with an alcohol and a little concentrated H₂SO₄. The acid and alcohol used were:
questions.x: CH₃CO– comes from ethanoic acid and –OCH₂CH₂CH₃ from propan-1-ol (propyl ethanoate). Propan-2-ol would give CH₃COOCH(CH₃)₂, and propanoic acid with ethanol gives the isomer CH₃CH₂COOCH₂CH₃.

questions.q: Which of the following is a secondary alcohol?
questions.x: In cyclohexanol the carbon bearing –OH is bonded to two ring carbons, so it is secondary. Benzyl alcohol and ethanol are primary; 2-methylpropan-2-ol is tertiary.

questions.q: Benzene reacts with ethanoyl chloride (CH₃COCl) in the presence of anhydrous AlCl₃. The product is:
questions.x: This is Friedel–Crafts acylation: the CH₃CO⁺ electrophile substitutes into the ring, giving the aromatic ketone phenylethanone (acetophenone) and HCl. Ethylbenzene would need an alkyl halide.

questions.q: In the base-catalysed addition of HCN to a carbonyl compound, the step that forms the new C–C bond is:
o: Attack of CN⁻ on the carbonyl carbon, giving an alkoxide ion
Attack of H⁺ on the carbonyl oxygen
Attack of CN⁻ on the carbonyl oxygen
Attack of HCN molecules on the α-carbon
questions.x: The cyanide ion, a nucleophile, attacks the δ+ carbonyl carbon and the π electrons move onto oxygen, forming an alkoxide ion. This then takes H⁺ from HCN, giving the cyanohydrin.

questions.q: Pure ethanoic acid is called glacial acetic acid because:
o: It freezes into ice-like crystals at about 17 °C
It is a colourless gas at room temperature
questions.x: Pure ethanoic acid has a freezing point of about 16.6 °C, so in cold weather it solidifies into an ice-like mass.

questions.q: Excess amino acids are not stored in the body. In the liver their amino groups are removed and the nitrogen is excreted mainly as:
questions.x: Deamination in the liver turns the amino nitrogen into urea, which the kidneys excrete. Glycogen is a stored carbohydrate and contains no nitrogen.

questions.q: Low-density polythene (LDPE) is less dense than high-density polythene (HDPE) because its chains:
o: Are cross-linked into a rigid network
Are highly branched and cannot pack closely
Are only about ten units long
questions.x: Branches keep LDPE chains apart, leaving more empty space, so the density is lower. HDPE has mostly straight chains that pack closely. Both are made of carbon and hydrogen only.

questions.q: Polythene softens when heated, but Bakelite does not. This is because Bakelite:
o: Is made of very short chains
questions.x: Bakelite is a thermosetting polymer whose chains are joined by cross-links, so heating cannot make them slide past each other. Polythene has separate chains and is thermoplastic. Bakelite is a condensation polymer.

questions.q: Using the cyclic rule for unit vectors, the cross product of k̂ with î (k̂ × î) gives:
questions.x: Following the cyclic order î → ĵ → k̂ → î: î × ĵ = k̂, ĵ × k̂ = î and k̂ × î = ĵ. Reversing the order would give −ĵ.

questions.q: On a displacement–time graph, a body moves from 0 m to 12 m in the first 3 s and then back to 0 m by t = 6 s, both along straight lines. Its average velocity and average speed over 6 s are:
questions.x: Net displacement is zero, so average velocity is zero. Total distance = 12 + 12 = 24 m, so average speed = 24 ÷ 6 = 4 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: Near the Earth's surface, the acceleration of a projectile (ignoring air resistance) is about:
questions.x: The only force is the projectile's weight, so it accelerates at g ≈ 9.8 m s⁻² straight down, like any freely falling body.

questions.q: For a projectile, the graphs of horizontal displacement against time and of vertical displacement against time are respectively:
o: A parabola and a straight line
A straight line and a parabola
questions.x: x = (v cos θ)t is linear in t, while y = (v sin θ)t − ½gt² contains t², so its graph is a parabola.

questions.q: Two bodies approach each other with a relative speed of 10 m s⁻¹ and collide head-on, perfectly elastically. Their relative speed of separation is:
questions.x: In a perfectly elastic collision the relative speed of separation equals the relative speed of approach, so it is 10 m s⁻¹.

questions.q: The displacement–time lines of two cars on the same road cross each other at one point. At that instant the two cars:
questions.x: Each point on a displacement–time graph gives position at a time, so the crossing point means both cars are at the same place at that instant. Equal velocity would need equal slopes.

questions.q: Taking zero potential energy at infinity, the gravitational potential energy of a satellite at a distance 2R from the Earth's centre (R = Earth's radius) compared with its value at the Earth's surface is:
o: Half in magnitude, and still negative
Twice in magnitude, and still negative
questions.x: Absolute PE = −GMm/r. At r = 2R it is −GMm/2R, half the surface value −GMm/R in magnitude, so it is greater (less negative) than at the surface. It is still negative; it only reaches zero at infinity.

questions.q: Two identical blocks are released from the same height, one down a smooth slope and one down a rough slope. At the bottom, the block on the rough slope has:
o: Less kinetic energy, the difference being the work done against friction
More kinetic energy, because friction pushes it along
The same kinetic energy as the other block
Zero kinetic energy in every case
questions.x: Both lose the same PE. On the rough slope part of it is dissipated as heat by friction, so less is left as kinetic energy.

questions.q: In most practical machines and devices, the energy that is wasted finally ends up mainly as:
o: Extra kinetic energy of the machine
Thermal energy spread into the surroundings
Gravitational potential energy of the parts
questions.x: Losses come mainly from friction, resistance and vibration, which all end up as heat that spreads into the surroundings and cannot easily be used again.

questions.q: A door swings open through a quarter turn. In radians this angle is:
questions.x: A full revolution is 2π rad, so one quarter of it is 2π/4 = π/2 rad (90°).

questions.q: A complete revolution, expressed in degrees, is:
questions.x: One complete revolution is 360°, which is the same as 2π rad. 57.3° is the size of one radian.

questions.q: For an ideal fluid flowing steadily through a pipe of varying cross-section, a graph of the flow speed v against 1/A (A = cross-sectional area) is:
o: A straight line parallel to the 1/A axis
A straight line through the origin
A curve that falls as 1/A increases
A straight line with negative slope
questions.x: Av = constant gives v = constant × (1/A), so v is directly proportional to 1/A: a straight line through the origin whose slope is the volume flow rate.

questions.q: You hold a strip of paper just below your lips so that it hangs down, and blow across its upper surface. The paper:
o: Swings away from your mouth and drops
questions.x: The fast-moving air above the paper is at lower pressure than the still air below, so the pressure difference lifts the paper.

questions.q: A weakened section of an artery wall bulges outward, widening the vessel there. By continuity and Bernoulli's principle, in the widened section the blood:
o: Speeds up and its pressure falls, so the wall collapses
Slows down and its pressure rises, which pushes the wall out further
Slows down and its pressure falls
Keeps the same speed and pressure
questions.x: A larger area means a lower speed (Av = constant), and lower speed means higher pressure (Bernoulli). The higher pressure tends to enlarge the bulge further.

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end is sounding its first overtone. Including the ends, the air column has:
questions.x: The first overtone of a closed pipe has L = 3λ/4: a node at the closed end, then an antinode, a node, and an antinode at the open end.

questions.q: A wave of amplitude 3 mm overlaps with a coherent wave of amplitude 4 mm. Depending on the point, the combined vibration has different sizes. Which value is impossible for the combined amplitude?
questions.x: The combined amplitude ranges from 4 − 3 = 1 mm (opposite phase) to 4 + 3 = 7 mm (in phase). 8 mm is outside that range; 5 mm occurs at an intermediate phase difference.

questions.q: At a certain instant, the resultant displacement at a point where two waves overlap is zero. This means that at that instant:
o: Both waves have stopped at that point
Neither wave has reached that point
The two waves have destroyed each other's energy
The two individual displacements are equal and opposite
questions.x: Superposition adds the displacements, so a zero total means they are equal in size and opposite in sign. Both waves are still present and carry on afterwards.

questions.q: Laplace's correction to Newton's formula concerned Newton's assumption about:
o: The density of air at STP
The thermal conditions of the compressions and rarefactions
The frequency of the sound wave
The amplitude of the sound wave
questions.x: Newton assumed the changes were isothermal; Laplace showed they are adiabatic, so the elastic modulus should be γP instead of P.

questions.q: A pulse travelling along a rope reaches an end that is tied firmly to a wall. The reflected pulse is:
o: Inverted, so an upward pulse returns as a downward pulse
Upright, with exactly the same shape
questions.x: At a fixed end the rope cannot move, so the pulse is reflected inverted (a phase change of π). It travels back at the same speed.

questions.q: If v₀ is the speed of sound in air at 0 °C, the speed at t °C is:
questions.x: v ∝ √T with T = 273 + t in kelvin, so v = v₀√((273 + t)/273) = v₀√(1 + t/273). Leaving out the square root, or using t in °C directly, is wrong.

questions.q: When gas is released quickly from an aerosol can, the can becomes cold. The best explanation is that the escaping gas:
o: Absorbs heat from the air and so cools down
Does work in expanding, using some of its internal energy
Gains internal energy from the can
Loses mass, which lowers its temperature
questions.x: The expansion is too fast for much heat to flow in, so the work done by the gas comes from its internal energy, and its temperature falls.

questions.q: A substance with a high specific heat is one that:
o: Needs a lot of heat to raise the temperature of each kilogram by 1 K
Heats up very quickly when given a little heat
questions.x: Specific heat is the heat needed per kilogram per kelvin. A high value means much heat is needed for a small temperature rise.

questions.q: Warming 0.2 kg of cooking oil through 15 K takes how many joules, if the oil's specific heat is 2000 J kg⁻¹ K⁻¹?
questions.x: Q = mcΔT = 0.2 × 2000 × 15 = 6000 J. Using 2 kg instead of 0.2 kg gives the wrong 60 000 J.

questions.q: The electronvolt (eV) is a unit of:
questions.x: 1 eV is the energy gained by an electron moving through a potential difference of 1 V, i.e. 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Despite the name, it is not a unit of potential.

questions.q: To make the electrostatic force between two fixed point charges four times as strong, the distance between them must be:
questions.x: F ∝ 1/r², so F becomes 4 times larger when r² becomes 4 times smaller, i.e. when r is halved.

questions.q: Charges +q and −q are a distance d apart. Compared with the field due to +q alone, the net field at the midpoint between them is:
questions.x: At the midpoint, the field of +q points towards −q and the field of −q also points towards −q. They are equal in size and add, so the field is doubled.

questions.q: The greatest power that a source of emf E and internal resistance r can deliver to an external load is:
questions.x: Maximum power transfer occurs when R = r. Then I = E/2r and P = I²R = (E²/4r²) × r = E²/4r.

questions.q: A wire of resistance 8 Ω is folded exactly in half and the two halves are twisted together to form a thicker wire. Its new resistance is:
questions.x: Folding halves the length (R halves) and doubles the cross-sectional area (R halves again), so R becomes 8 ÷ 4 = 2 Ω.

questions.q: The period of the circular motion of an ion of mass m and charge q circling in a uniform field B is:
questions.x: T = 2πr/v and r = mv/(qB), so T = 2πm/(qB). The speed cancels out.

questions.q: The correct order in which electricity passes from a power station to a home is:
o: Generator, step-up transformer, transmission lines, step-down transformer
Generator, step-down transformer, transmission lines, step-up transformer
Generator, transmission lines, step-up transformer, step-down transformer
Generator, step-up transformer, step-down transformer, transmission lines
questions.x: Voltage is raised by a step-up transformer at the station, carried on the lines at high voltage, and lowered by step-down transformers near homes.

questions.q: Two electromagnetic waves in a vacuum have frequencies 10¹⁵ Hz and 10¹⁸ Hz. The ratio of the wavelength of the first to that of the second is:
questions.x: All EM waves travel at c in a vacuum, so λ = c/f and λ₁/λ₂ = f₂/f₁ = 10¹⁸/10¹⁵ = 1000.

questions.q: A full-wave rectifier works from 50 Hz mains. What is the time interval between the starts of successive output pulses?
questions.x: Full-wave output has 2 × 50 = 100 pulses per second, so one pulse every 1/100 s = 10 ms. 20 ms would be the half-wave value.

questions.q: Ultraviolet light of wavelength 330 nm falls on a surface. How much energy does each photon deliver? (h = 6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ J s, c = 3 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹)
questions.x: E = hc/λ = (6.6 × 10⁻³⁴ × 3 × 10⁸)/(3.3 × 10⁻⁷) = 6 × 10⁻¹⁹ J. Forgetting to convert nm to m gives the 10⁻²⁸ value.

questions.q: The series limit, the shortest-wavelength line of the Balmer series, corresponds to the transition:
questions.x: The largest energy drop within the Balmer series is from n = ∞ to n = 2, giving the shortest wavelength. n = ∞ to n = 1 is the Lyman series limit.

questions.q: A source has an activity of 1200 Bq. Its half-life is 6 hours. Its activity 18 hours later will be:
questions.x: 18 hours is 3 half-lives: 1200 → 600 → 300 → 150 Bq. Dividing by 3 instead of halving three times gives 400.

questions.q: Gamma sources in hospitals are stored in thick lead containers because lead:
o: Converts gamma rays into harmless alpha particles
Is the only material gamma rays cannot reach
Absorbs gamma radiation strongly due to its high density
questions.x: Dense, high-atomic-number materials such as lead absorb gamma rays well, cutting the dose outside. Nothing changes the source's rate of decay.

questions.q: To make kheer for six people, wash half a cup of rice and soak it for an hour. Then boil it slowly in a litre of milk for forty minutes, stirring often so that it does not stick. Add sugar and cardamom and cook for ten minutes more. Finally, let the kheer cool for two hours before serving it, topped with chopped almonds. According to the passage, how long does it take from the start of soaking until the kheer is ready to serve?
questions.x: Soaking 1 hour + boiling 40 minutes + cooking 10 minutes + cooling 2 hours = 3 hours 50 minutes. Leaving out the ten extra minutes of cooking gives the tempting 3 hours 40 minutes.

questions.q: "With great effort, the farmer dragged an enormous log out of the canal." The closest synonym of 'enormous' is:
questions.x: 'Enormous' means very large, so 'huge' is the synonym; 'heavy' describes weight, not size.

questions.q: "Sara is usually gregarious and chats with everyone, but at the funeral she sat alone and spoke to no one." The word 'gregarious' means:
questions.x: 'Gregarious' means sociable, fond of being with others; the contrast word 'but' and 'chats with everyone' point to this meaning.

questions.q: Choose the correct verb: "When I met Bilal at the wedding last week, I hardly recognised him because I ___ him for ten years."
questions.x: The ten years without seeing him came before a past event (the wedding), so the past perfect 'had not seen' is needed.

questions.q: Where should the comma go in a sentence that begins with a long introductory phrase?
o: After, the long journey from Gilgit the travellers rested.
After the long journey, from Gilgit the travellers rested.
After the long journey from Gilgit the, travellers rested.
After the long journey from Gilgit, the travellers rested.
questions.x: The comma goes at the end of the introductory phrase, just before the main clause begins.

questions.q: How many clauses are there in "When the rain stopped, the children went out and they played until it got dark"?
questions.x: There are two subordinate clauses ('When the rain stopped', 'until it got dark') and two main clauses ('the children went out', 'they played').

questions.q: Choose the correct pronoun: "The doctor and the nurse explained ___ plan to the patient's family."
questions.x: Two antecedents joined by 'and' form a plural, so the plural pronoun 'their' is required.

questions.q: Choose the correct spelling to fill the blank: "It is a great ____ to study at this medical college."
questions.x: The correct spelling is 'privilege': p-r-i-v-i-l-e-g-e, with no 'd' and with 'i' then 'e' in the middle syllables.

questions.q: Which sentence correctly combines "The doctor was very kind." and "She treated my mother."?
o: The doctor who treated my mother was very kind.
The doctor which treated my mother was very kind.
The doctor whom treated my mother was very kind.
The doctor, she treated my mother, was very kind.
questions.x: 'Who' is the relative pronoun for a person acting as subject. 'Which' is for things, 'whom' is an object form, and the last version adds an extra pronoun 'she'.

questions.q: Kamran believes that antibiotics will cure his common cold because antibiotics kill bacteria. Why is his belief false?
o: The common cold is caused by viruses, which antibiotics do not kill
The common cold is caused by bacteria that resist all medicines
questions.x: Antibiotics act against bacteria, but a common cold is a viral infection. His reasoning starts from a true fact and applies it to the wrong kind of germ.

questions.q: Find the next letter: Z, Y, W, T, P, ?
questions.x: The steps back grow by one: -1, -2, -3, -4, so next is -5. P(16) - 5 = K(11).

questions.q: Find the next number: 2, 10, 50, 250, ?
questions.x: Each term is 5 times the one before: 250 x 5 = 1250.

questions.q: From the school gate, Kashif cycles 7 km due east. He then turns left for 5 km, turns left again for 7 km, and finally turns right for 3 km. How far is he from the gate, and in which direction?
questions.x: East 7 and later west 7 cancel out. He walks north 5 km and then, after the right turn from facing west, north 3 km more: 8 km north.

questions.q: If 5 March of a certain year is a Tuesday, what day of the week is 30 March of the same year?
questions.x: 30 March is 25 days after 5 March. 25 = 3 weeks + 4 days, and 4 days after Tuesday is Saturday.

questions.q: Statement: Crops in a village often fail because canal water reaches it at irregular times, although groundwater is available. Courses of action: I. Farmers should be helped to use groundwater, such as through tube wells, in a careful way. II. The irrigation department should set a regular water schedule for the village. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Using the available groundwater gives farmers a backup, and a regular canal schedule fixes the main problem. Both use the information given.

questions.q: Statement: A survey in a city finds that most dengue mosquito larvae are breeding in water collected in old tyres and uncovered water tanks. Courses of action: I. Citizens should be told to cover water tanks and empty or remove old tyres. II. Anti-mosquito spraying should be done only in the city's parks. Which course(s) of action follow?
questions.x: Action I targets exactly where the survey found the larvae. Action II ignores the data, since parks were not named as the main breeding sites.

questions.q: Which belief can be rejected because there is no possible cause-and-effect link?
o: Covering food keeps flies away from it
Washing fruit removes some dirt and germs
Hanging a lemon and chillies at a shop door keeps losses away
Wearing a seat belt reduces injury in a crash
questions.x: Lemons and chillies have no way of affecting a shop's business. The other three describe real causes and effects.

questions.q: Usman scored poorly in his first mock test and says, "I am not smart enough to become a doctor." Which argument most strongly challenges his belief?
o: Mock tests are always easier than the real exam
One mock test shows what he needs to work on, and many students raise their scores through regular practice
He should stop taking mock tests
Becoming a doctor depends only on luck
questions.x: A single low score is feedback, not proof of ability. Steady practice usually improves results, so his conclusion goes far beyond the evidence.
